templates.scenario: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a} and want to move up. A mentor asks you to write one goal for the next six months, and you drafted four versions.
templates.prompt: Which goal is the most useful for guiding your progress?

options.text: Finish the first level of a job-related certification course by the end of next semester by studying three hours each week.
options.why: This goal is specific, measurable, realistic and has a deadline and a plan, so you will know whether you reached it.

options.text: Learn everything there is to know about this field as quickly as I possibly can over the next several months.
options.why: This goal is too broad and has no way to measure success. It is not realistic to learn everything, so it is hard to know when you have made progress.
options.misconception: A bigger goal is always a better goal.

options.text: Earn a job-related certification someday soon by working hard and staying focused on my studies.
options.why: 'Someday soon' is not a deadline and 'working hard' is not a measure. A goal needs a date and a way to check progress.
options.misconception: Effort alone makes a goal useful.

options.text: Become the best employee in the entire company and get promoted before anyone else at my level.
options.why: 'Best' depends on other people's opinions and cannot be measured by you. A goal should focus on something you control.
options.misconception: Competing with others is the best way to set a goal.

templates.principle: Useful goals are specific, measurable, realistic and tied to a date, with a plan for reaching them.

review.notes: No policy needed; goals are hypothetical.

templates.scenario: The benefits packet at {workplace|the} says employees can use a free, confidential counseling program. For several weeks you have felt constantly stressed about balancing work and school, and it is affecting your sleep.
templates.prompt: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Read the benefits packet details and contact the program, along with the supports you already trust.
options.why: Using a resource your workplace provides is a healthy way to manage stress, and combining it with people you trust gives you more than one support.

options.text: Keep pushing through until the school term ends, then think about how you are feeling.
options.why: Ongoing stress that affects sleep is worth addressing now. Waiting for a convenient time can let it grow.
options.misconception: Stress will go away on its own once things get quieter.

options.text: Ask coworkers to cover your shifts for a while without telling anyone why you need the time.
options.why: Asking others to cover without explanation can strain your team and does not address what is causing the stress.
options.misconception: Time off without explanation solves stress.

options.text: Wait until the stress begins affecting your work performance before using any kind of support.
options.why: Support is meant to be used before problems become serious. Waiting for performance to suffer makes everything harder.
options.misconception: Support is only for serious situations.

templates.principle: Know the support your workplace provides and use it early to manage stress and well-being.

review.notes: Program existence stated from the benefits packet in the scenario; no medical advice given.

templates.scenario: You just received your first paycheck from {workplace|the}. It is smaller than you expected, and the pay stub lists several deductions that you do not recognize.

options.text: Read the pay stub line by line, and ask payroll or your {lead} about any deduction that is unclear.
options.why: Understanding what each deduction is comes before any decision about money. Asking about the ones you do not know avoids acting on a wrong assumption.

options.text: Spend the money right away on things you have been wanting, since you earned it.
options.why: Spending before understanding what you received makes it hard to plan. A smaller check may mean you have less available than you expected.
options.misconception: The amount I earned is the amount I can spend.

options.text: Assume the paycheck is a mistake and demand a corrected check from your {lead} the same day.
options.why: Deductions are common, and demanding a correction before reading the stub can lead to an awkward mix-up. Check first, then ask.
options.misconception: A smaller check always means an error.

options.text: Make a budget based on the full amount shown at the top of the stub, ignoring what you actually received.
options.why: Budgets should be built on money you actually have. Gross pay is not what arrives in your account.
options.misconception: Gross pay is what I actually earn.

templates.principle: Read your pay stub before making money decisions, and ask about anything you do not understand.

review.notes: No claims about specific deductions or laws; generic budgeting principle.

templates.timing: Understanding the deductions has to come before budgeting or complaining.

templates.scenario: You are interested in a new role at {workplace|the} and want to plan how to get there.
templates.prompt: Put these planning steps in a sensible order.

steps.text: Find out what the new role requires
Compare those requirements with your current skills
Make a plan to build any skills you are missing

precedence.why: You cannot compare yourself with the role until you know what it asks.
Knowing the gaps tells you what to work on.
Applying after you have a plan to build your skills gives you a stronger case.

templates.principle: Plan a career move by learning the requirements, finding your gaps, building skills, and then applying.

review.notes: A natural chain; no legal content.

templates.scenario: A student worker at {workplace|the} writes this plan.
templates.prompt: Tap the line that is a problem.
templates.docTitle: My plan for finishing the certification

segments.text: My goal is to finish my certification by June.
segments.whyFine: A clear goal with a date.

segments.text: I will study two evenings each week.
segments.whyFine: A realistic, specific part of the plan.

segments.text: I will also work every weekend and stay up late most nights, since I can catch up on sleep after June.
segments.why: Giving up sleep for months is not sustainable and can hurt health and performance. A good plan protects well-being.

segments.text: I will check my progress at the end of each month.
segments.whyFine: Regular check-ins keep a goal on track.

templates.principle: A good plan includes rest and well-being; goals that rely on constant exhaustion are unlikely to last.

review.notes: Single line trades health for a goal; no medical claims beyond sustainability.
